title: Schedule II Faxes and Multiple Prescriptions, Schedule III-V Partial Fills, Massachusetts Supply Ceilings, Endorsement, Retention and Narcotic Treatment Limits
topic: Controlled substance prescriptions / Fax originals, multiple Schedule II prescriptions and their Massachusetts validity, Schedule III-V partial filling, Massachusetts single-filling supply ceilings, Schedule II endorsement and filing, prescription retention, and narcotic treatment limits
subtopic: When a faxed Schedule II prescription is only an advance copy and when it serves as the original under 21 CFR 1306.11(a) and (e)-(g); multiple Schedule II prescriptions under 21 CFR 1306.12(b), their dating under 21 CFR 1306.05(a), the pharmacist's earliest-fill duty under 21 CFR 1306.14(e), and the Massachusetts 30-day validity under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) as Massachusetts guidance applies it to do-not-fill-before dates; partial filling of Schedule III-V prescriptions under 21 CFR 1306.23; the single-filling supply ceilings in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d) and Board Policy 2024-05; the filling pharmacist's endorsement and the separate file for written Schedule II prescriptions under s. 23(b) and (c); two-year retention under s. 23(e); and the limits in 21 CFR 1306.07 on administering, dispensing, prescribing and delivering narcotic drugs for maintenance or detoxification treatment, with the Massachusetts limits on a practitioner's own dispensing to an ultimate user in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(b) and 105 CMR 700.010(A)
learning_objectives: Distinguish a faxed Schedule II prescription that is only an advance copy under 21 CFR 1306.11(a) from one that serves as the original written prescription under paragraph (e), (f) or (g).
Match each fax-as-original paragraph to its drug condition, its patient or setting condition and any notation it requires, and identify the one paragraph that does not require a narcotic substance.
State the five conditions on which an individual practitioner may issue multiple Schedule II prescriptions under 21 CFR 1306.12(b), and explain what a pharmacy may and may not do with the set.
State how every prescription in a multiple Schedule II set is dated under 21 CFR 1306.05(a), and what 21 CFR 1306.14(e) forbids a pharmacist to do with a later prescription in the set.
Apply the Massachusetts 30-day validity period to each prescription in a multiple Schedule II set, measuring it as Massachusetts guidance does from the do-not-fill-before date.
Apply the three conditions of 21 CFR 1306.23 to a staged dispensing of a Schedule III, IV or V prescription, counting the six months from the date the prescription was issued.
Classify a Schedule II or III prescription into a 90-day category or the 30-day default under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d) and Policy 2024-05, and say whom the ceiling binds.
Identify the filling pharmacist's endorsement duty under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(c) and the separate-file requirement for written Schedule II prescriptions under s. 23(b).
Apply the two-year retention rule in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(e), recognising what the subsection does not say and the course that is safe where it is silent.

Sort maintenance and detoxification treatment under 21 CFR 1306.07 by schedule, actor and action, apply the limits on the three-day dispensing provision in paragraph (b), and apply the conditions in paragraph (f) to a pharmacy's delivery of a Schedule III, IV or V narcotic drug for injection or implantation, together with the Massachusetts limits on a practitioner's own dispensing in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(b) and 105 CMR 700.010(A).
Layer the Massachusetts rules over each federal provision in this section and decide which governs where both reach the same act.

orientation.text: 21 CFR 1306.11(a) starts from a strict default. A pharmacist may dispense directly a Schedule II controlled substance that is a prescription drug only pursuant to a written prescription signed by the practitioner, except as provided in paragraph (d), the emergency oral route taught with emergency oral Schedule II dispensing and its follow-up. The same paragraph allows a paper Schedule II prescription to be transmitted by the practitioner or the practitioner's agent to a pharmacy by facsimile, provided that the original manually signed prescription is presented to the pharmacist for review prior to the actual dispensing, except as noted in paragraphs (e), (f) and (g). Read with that proviso, an ordinary fax is an advance copy. Because the condition attaches to the actual dispensing, the fax can reach the pharmacy and be worked on before the original arrives, but it does not replace the original: nothing is dispensed until the pharmacist has reviewed the original manually signed prescription, which is maintained in accordance with 21 CFR 1304.04(h). The senders the paragraph names are the practitioner and the practitioner's agent.

Paragraphs (e), (f) and (g) are the three situations in which the fax itself serves as the original written prescription, and each is keyed to a different combination of drug and patient. In each of them the prescription is prepared in accordance with 21 CFR 1306.05, it is transmitted by the practitioner or the practitioner's agent, and the facsimile is maintained in accordance with 21 CFR 1304.04(h). Paragraph (e) covers a Schedule II narcotic substance to be compounded for the direct administration to a patient by parenteral, intravenous, intramuscular, subcutaneous or intraspinal infusion; it names no setting, so nothing in it turns on where the patient is, but a drug that is not a narcotic, or one that is not to be compounded for one of those routes, falls outside it. Paragraph (f) covers a Schedule II substance for a resident of a Long Term Care Facility and, unlike (e) and (g), does not require a narcotic, so a stimulant for a resident qualifies. Paragraph (g) covers a Schedule II narcotic substance for a patient enrolled in a hospice care program certified and/or paid for by Medicare under Title XVIII or a hospice program licensed by the state, and it adds that the practitioner or the practitioner's agent will note on the prescription that the patient is a hospice patient. The paragraph does not say what follows if that note is missing; the course that is safe on either reading is to treat the fax as the original only once a prescription carrying the note has come from the practitioner's side, and otherwise to wait for the original.

A federal fax exception answers one question: whether, for federal purposes, the facsimile may stand as the original written prescription. It does not decide whether a Massachusetts pharmacy may accept a Schedule II prescription in written or faxed form at all. That question turns on the Massachusetts electronic-prescribing requirement, its exceptions and the Massachusetts written-format rules, which are taught with Massachusetts oral prescriptions together with how faxed and telephoned prescriptions are received, and where the federal and Massachusetts rules both reach the same prescription the stricter one governs. Two Massachusetts duties taught later in this section also bear on a Schedule II prescription received by fax: the pharmacist filling a written or electronic Schedule II prescription endorses his or her own signature on its face, and written Schedule II prescriptions are kept in a separate file. Because the federal text makes a qualifying facsimile the original written prescription, keeping it in that separate file satisfies the filing sentence on any reading.

21 CFR 1306.12 opens by prohibiting the refilling of a prescription for a Schedule II controlled substance, and paragraph (b) then supplies the lawful way to cover more than one period of therapy: separate prescriptions issued together. An individual practitioner may issue multiple prescriptions authorizing the patient to receive a total of up to a 90-day supply of a Schedule II controlled substance, provided five conditions are met. Each separate prescription is issued for a legitimate medical purpose by an individual practitioner acting in the usual course of professional practice. The practitioner provides written instructions on each prescription, other than the first if the practitioner intends that one to be filled immediately, indicating the earliest date on which a pharmacy may fill each prescription. The practitioner concludes that providing the patient with multiple prescriptions in this manner does not create an undue risk of diversion or abuse. The issuance of multiple prescriptions is permissible under the applicable state laws. And the practitioner complies fully with all other applicable requirements under the Act and the regulations, as well as any additional requirements under state law. Paragraph (b)(2) adds that nothing in paragraph (b) mandates or encourages issuing multiple prescriptions or seeing patients only once every 90 days; whether to do so is for the practitioner's own sound medical judgment in accordance with established medical standards.

Two further federal provisions answer questions the multiple-prescription paragraph leaves to them. 21 CFR 1306.05(a) requires all prescriptions for controlled substances to be dated as of, and signed on, the day when issued, so every prescription in a set issued at one visit bears the date of that visit; a later prescription is not held back by giving it a later date. What holds it back is the practitioner's written instruction, and 21 CFR 1306.14(e) turns that instruction into a duty on the pharmacist: where a prescription prepared in accordance with 1306.12(b) contains instructions from the prescribing practitioner indicating that it shall not be filled until a certain date, no pharmacist may fill it before that date. Every condition in 1306.12(b) is addressed to the individual practitioner who issues the prescriptions, so a pharmacist cannot create a set by splitting one prescription into several, and the later prescriptions are separate prescriptions rather than refills of the first. The 90 days is a ceiling on the total the set may authorize, not an allowance for each prescription in it. Paragraphs (b)(1)(iv) and (v) then make the whole permission depend on state law, which in Massachusetts brings in both the validity period of a Schedule II prescription and the single-filling supply ceilings.

Massachusetts adds a clock of its own. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) a written or electronic prescription for a controlled substance in Schedule II becomes invalid 30 days after the date of issuance. The subsection does not itself say what the date of issuance is for a prescription that carries a do-not-fill-before date, and a candidate who counts from the date written would conclude that the later prescriptions in a 90-day set expire before they can be filled. Massachusetts guidance answers the question the other way. A Board of Registration in Medicine guideline, concurring with the joint policy of the Drug Control Program and the Board of Registration in Pharmacy, records their determination that issuing multiple Schedule II prescriptions in accordance with the federal regulation is permissible under chapter 94C, and states that the date of issuance referred to in section 23 shall be the do-not-fill-before date indicated by the prescriber, while the date written is the date the prescription was written and signed; accordingly each written prescription becomes invalid 30 days after its date of issuance. The Board of Registration in Pharmacy's December 2025 newsletter says the same of a Massachusetts prescriber's Schedule II prescriptions, which it describes as valid for 30 days from the date of issuance or the do-not-fill-before date, as applicable, adding that because prescriptions may not be post-dated the clock starts from the later do-not-fill-before date where there is one. A later prescription in a set can therefore be filled in Massachusetts on or after its do-not-fill-before date and before it becomes invalid 30 days after that date, while a prescription with no such date becomes invalid 30 days after the date it was issued. The same guideline reports DEA's interpretation that no verbal modifications can be made to the earliest date on which the Schedule II prescription may be filled. Prescriptions from practitioners outside Massachusetts run on different periods, taught with out-of-state prescriptions, and the same question arises there. A Schedule II prescription from an out-of-state practitioner filled under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d) or (d1/2) may be filled only if it was issued within the preceding five days, and those subsections do not say how a do-not-fill-before date bears on that period. The Board of Registration in Pharmacy's December 2025 newsletter answers it the same way, describing a nonresident prescriber's Schedule II prescriptions as only valid for five days from the date of issuance or the do-not-fill-before date, as applicable. On that guidance a later prescription in such a set does not lapse before its do-not-fill-before date arrives: its five days run from that date, and the other out-of-state conditions still apply.

Schedule III, IV and V prescriptions have a partial-filling rule of their own, and it is much shorter than the rules that govern Schedule II. Under 21 CFR 1306.23 the partial filling of a prescription for a controlled substance listed in Schedule III, IV or V is permissible, provided that each partial filling is recorded in the same manner as a refilling, the total quantity dispensed in all partial fillings does not exceed the total quantity prescribed, and no dispensing occurs after 6 months after the date on which the prescription was issued. The section attaches no condition to who asks for a partial filling or why, and it sets no number of partial fillings; what it controls is the aggregate and the calendar. The six months run from the date of issue, not from the first partial filling, so staging the quantity never buys more time, and splitting it never creates more quantity. How a refilling is recorded, and the refill and transfer limits themselves, are taught with Schedule III-V refills and transfers; Schedule II partial fills, including the Massachusetts 30-day ceiling on filling the remainder, run on different rules taught in their own section. For a Schedule III prescription filled in Massachusetts, each partial filling is still a filling, so the single-filling supply ceiling in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d) applies to it.

Massachusetts limits how much of a Schedule II or III substance may be dispensed at once, and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d) states the limit as a supply upon a single filling. Unless otherwise prohibited by statute, prescriptions for Schedule II or III controlled substances may be filled for a maximum of a 90-day supply upon a single filling in three categories: (i) the treatment of opioid use disorder, including, but not limited to, buprenorphine; (ii) non-opioid controlled substances, including, but not limited to, methylphenidate and testosterone; and (iii) implantable infusion pumps. All other prescriptions for controlled substances in Schedule II or III may be filled for a maximum of a 30-day supply upon a single filling. The subsection speaks to the filling, so its ceilings bind whoever fills the prescription, and the figure measures the supply dispensed, not the time a prescription remains valid; the 30 days after which a Schedule II prescription becomes invalid under s. 23(a) is a different measure altogether. The 90 days is a maximum rather than an entitlement, and the opening words keep any stricter statutory limit in force, such as a limit on an initial opioid prescription where one applies. The subsection also lets the department provide by regulation that a Schedule II or III substance may be filled for a maximum of less than a 90-day supply upon a single filling, if the secretary of health and human services or the board of pharmacy determines that the restriction is needed to address increased abuse of the substance. It sets no single-filling maximum for Schedule IV or V.

The Board of Registration in Pharmacy and the Drug Control Program restate the subsection in Policy 2024-05, Schedules II and III Quantity Limits, adopted September 5, 2024. In the policy's words, Schedules II and III prescriptions may be written and filled for a 90-day supply for drugs for the treatment of opioid use disorder, such as buprenorphine products; any non-opioids in Schedules II and III, such as stimulants and testosterone; and implantable infusion pumps, while all other Schedule II and III medications, such as opioids, may only be filled for a maximum 30-day supply. The policy adds three practical points: the change applies to all pharmacies that dispense into, within, or from Massachusetts; there is no longer a need to verify diagnoses for narcolepsy, attention deficit disorder or attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder; and changes to prescriptions for federally controlled drugs must be discussed with the prescriber. Classification therefore comes before counting. Category (i) of the statute is described by what the prescription is for, category (ii) by what kind of drug it is, and category (iii) by how the drug is delivered, so a drug's schedule alone never places a prescription in a 90-day category. A buprenorphine product prescribed for pain is not, on the statute's terms, a prescription for the treatment of opioid use disorder, and buprenorphine is an opioid; because the policy lists buprenorphine products as its example of drugs for opioid use disorder, the course that is safe on either reading is to fill such a prescription for no more than a 30-day supply upon a single filling.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(b) and (c) put two handling duties on the Schedule II prescriptions a Massachusetts pharmacy fills, beside a Massachusetts statement of the no-refill rule. Section 23(c) provides that the pharmacist filling a written or electronic prescription for a controlled substance in Schedule II shall endorse his own signature on the face thereof. The duty belongs to the filling pharmacist personally: the prescriber's signature is a different thing, initials on a label are not a signature on the face of the prescription, and a technician is not the filling pharmacist. The subsection names electronic prescriptions expressly but does not say how the face of an electronic prescription is endorsed. What it does settle is that the electronic form is no exemption, and the course that is safe on any reading is for the filling pharmacist's own signature to be endorsed on the electronic prescription record rather than left off. Section 23(b) provides that a written or electronic Schedule II prescription shall not be refilled, and that written Schedule II prescriptions shall be kept in a separate file. The filing sentence speaks only of written prescriptions and names no actor; it is satisfied by keeping written Schedule II prescriptions in a file of their own.

Section 23(e) supplies the Massachusetts retention rule for the prescriptions themselves: all prescriptions for controlled substances shall be kept for two years by the pharmacy and shall be subject to inspection pursuant to the provisions of chapter 94C. The actor is the pharmacy, the object is every prescription for a controlled substance, and the subsection states no exception. It also does not say from what event the two years are counted. The course that is safe on any reading is to count from the last dispensing made on the prescription, which cannot fall before its issue date or its first filling. Retention runs on its own clock: a prescription that can no longer be filled or refilled still has to be kept, and a newer prescription for the same patient does not retire an older one. Which drugs chapter 94C treats as controlled substances, including whether its sixth schedule counts, is settled by the chapter's own definitions and schedules, covered in the schedule overview. The federal record-retention floor and the way it is measured are taught with inventories and records; where both reach the same prescription, the pharmacy keeps it until the later of the two periods has run.

21 CFR 1306.07 governs narcotic drugs used for maintenance or detoxification treatment of a narcotic dependent person, and it sorts the lawful routes by schedule. Under paragraph (a), a practitioner may administer or dispense directly, but not prescribe, a narcotic drug in Schedule II to a narcotic dependent person for the purpose of maintenance or detoxification treatment if the practitioner is separately registered with DEA as a narcotic treatment program and is in compliance with DEA regulations regarding treatment qualifications, security, records, and unsupervised use of the drugs. Under paragraph (d), a practitioner may administer or dispense, including prescribe, any Schedule III, IV or V narcotic drug for use in maintenance or detoxification treatment to a narcotic dependent person. No paragraph of the section provides for prescribing a Schedule II narcotic drug for maintenance or detoxification treatment: paragraphs (a) and (b) both exclude prescribing, and the paragraphs that involve prescriptions, (d) and (f), are confined to Schedules III, IV and V. A community pharmacy presented with a prescription for methadone, a Schedule II narcotic, whose purpose is maintenance or detoxification treatment therefore finds no route in 1306.07 for filling it as an ordinary Schedule II prescription, while a buprenorphine prescription for the same purpose falls within paragraph (d). Purpose is the hinge: the limits are written around maintenance and detoxification treatment, and methadone prescribed for pain is dispensed under the ordinary Schedule II rules. How a pharmacist may administer medication within an opioid treatment program is covered in its own section.

Paragraph (b) is the narrow provision for a practitioner who is not specifically registered to conduct a narcotic treatment program, and its conditions are cumulative. The practitioner may dispense, but not prescribe, narcotic drugs, in accordance with applicable Federal, State, and local laws relating to controlled substances, to one person or for one person's use at one time, for the purpose of initiating maintenance treatment or detoxification treatment or both. Not more than a three-day supply of the medication may be dispensed to the person or for the person's use at one time while arrangements are being made for referral for treatment, and such emergency treatment may not be renewed or extended. The paragraph is a bridge to referral, not a way of carrying a patient: a further supply once the first has been dispensed renews or extends the emergency treatment, and a prescription is outside the paragraph altogether.

Two further paragraphs mark the edges of the section. Paragraph (c) states that the section is not intended to impose any limitations on a physician or authorized hospital staff to administer or dispense narcotic drugs in a hospital to maintain or detoxify a person as an incidental adjunct to medical or surgical treatment of conditions other than addiction, or to administer or dispense narcotic drugs to persons with intractable pain in which no relief or cure is possible or none has been found after reasonable efforts. Paragraph (f), notwithstanding the Act's definition of dispense, lets a pharmacy deliver a controlled substance to a practitioner, pursuant to a prescription that meets the requirements of 21 CFR 1306.04, for administration by the practitioner, if six conditions are met: delivery to the prescribing practitioner or the administering practitioner at the location listed on the practitioner's DEA certificate of registration; a narcotic drug in Schedule III, IV or V to be administered for maintenance or detoxification treatment by injection or implantation; authority for the pharmacy and each practitioner to conduct those activities under the law of the State in which they take place; a prescription not issued to supply any practitioner with a stock of controlled substances for general dispensing to patients; administration only to the patient named on the prescription not later than 45 days after the date the practitioner receives the substance; and complete and accurate records, kept by the prescribing and administering practitioners as applicable, of all controlled substances delivered, received, administered or otherwise disposed of under the paragraph, including the persons to whom they were delivered.

Massachusetts adds more than a quantity ceiling. Paragraph (b) allows its three-day dispensing only in accordance with applicable Federal, State, and local laws, and two Massachusetts provisions reach a practitioner's own dispensing to a patient. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(b) lets the practitioners it lists, acting in good faith, dispense by delivering to an ultimate user a controlled substance in a single dose or in a quantity that is, in the practitioner's opinion, essential for the treatment of a patient, but the amount dispensed shall not exceed the quantity necessary for the immediate and proper treatment of the patient until it is possible for the patient to have a prescription filled by a pharmacy, and all controlled substances required by the patient as part of the patient's treatment shall be dispensed by prescription to the ultimate user in accordance with chapter 94C. The Department's regulation is narrower still. Under 105 CMR 700.010(A), other than for immediate administration, a practitioner shall not dispense controlled substances to an ultimate user in the course of professional practice except as sample medications, and for Schedule II through V the exception is a sample medication in a single dose or in such quantity as in the practitioner's opinion is essential for the immediate treatment of the patient; a sample medication is, under 105 CMR 700.001, a unit of prescription drug distributed by the manufacturer or distributor to practitioners in the original package from the manufacturer, not repackaged and given free of charge to patients. A take-home supply of methadone that a Massachusetts office practitioner counts out of the office's stock is repackaged and is not a sample medication, so the regulation does not allow it, whatever 21 CFR 1306.07(b) permits as a federal matter, and where both reach the same act the stricter rule governs; the regulation states its bar as applying other than for immediate administration. Massachusetts also sets a ceiling on pharmacy fillings. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d) a Schedule II or III prescription for the treatment of opioid use disorder, including buprenorphine, may be filled for a maximum of a 90-day supply upon a single filling unless otherwise prohibited by statute. That ceiling operates on a prescription that may lawfully be issued and filled. It applies to a buprenorphine prescription written under 21 CFR 1306.07(d), but it cannot make fillable a prescription for a Schedule II narcotic drug for maintenance or detoxification treatment for which 1306.07 provides no route.
