worked_examples.scenario: On one morning a pharmacy that serves long-term care facilities, hospice patients and home infusion patients receives four faxed Schedule II prescriptions, each sent by a prescriber's office and otherwise complete: methylphenidate tablets for a resident of a long-term care facility; oxycodone tablets for a patient living at home who is enrolled in a Medicare-certified hospice program, with no hospice notation on the prescription; hydromorphone to be compounded for continuous subcutaneous infusion for a patient at home; and oxycodone tablets for an ambulatory clinic patient. A technician proposes to dispense all four from the faxes.
steps: Start from the default in 21 CFR 1306.11(a): a faxed paper Schedule II prescription may arrive ahead of the original, but the original manually signed prescription must be presented to the pharmacist for review prior to the actual dispensing unless paragraph (e), (f) or (g) applies.

The methylphenidate fits paragraph (f), which reaches a Schedule II substance for a resident of a Long Term Care Facility. That paragraph does not require a narcotic, so the stimulant qualifies and the fax serves as the original written prescription.

The hospice oxycodone fits paragraph (g) on drug and patient: oxycodone is a Schedule II narcotic, the patient is enrolled in a Medicare-certified hospice program, and the paragraph names no residence. But paragraph (g) also provides that the practitioner or the practitioner's agent will note on the prescription that the patient is a hospice patient, and this prescription carries no such note. The course that is safe on either reading is to obtain a prescription carrying the note from the prescriber's side, or the original, before dispensing.

The hydromorphone fits paragraph (e): a Schedule II narcotic substance to be compounded for direct administration to the patient by subcutaneous infusion. Paragraph (e) names no setting, so the patient's being at home changes nothing, and the fax serves as the original.
The clinic oxycodone meets none of the three paragraphs. Its fax is an advance copy, and the pharmacist must review the original manually signed prescription before the actual dispensing.

Each fax that serves as the original is maintained in accordance with 21 CFR 1304.04(h). On Massachusetts facts, whether the pharmacy may accept a non-electronic Schedule II prescription at all is decided under the Massachusetts electronic-prescribing and written-format rules taught with Massachusetts oral prescriptions, and the stricter rule governs.
worked_examples.resolution: The methylphenidate and hydromorphone faxes may be dispensed as originals; the hospice oxycodone should wait for a prescription carrying the hospice note or for the original; and the clinic oxycodone cannot be dispensed until the pharmacist has reviewed the original manually signed prescription. The error the scenario invites is treating the three fax exceptions as interchangeable: carrying the narcotic condition into the facility exception, dropping the notation from the hospice exception, or reading any Schedule II fax as an original.

worked_examples.scenario: On 3 March a Massachusetts prescriber issues a patient three separate Schedule II prescriptions for methylphenidate, each for a 30-day supply and each dated 3 March. The first is meant to be filled that day; the second carries a written instruction not to fill it before 2 April, and the third not before 2 May. The patient fills the first on 3 March, returns on 25 March asking to fill the second early before a trip, and presents the third on 12 May. A technician says the third expired in early April because it was written on 3 March, and the patient asks whether the prescriber could simply telephone the pharmacy with an earlier date for the second.
steps: The set fits 21 CFR 1306.12(b): an individual practitioner may issue multiple Schedule II prescriptions authorizing a total of up to a 90-day supply, with written instructions on each prescription other than a first intended for immediate filling indicating the earliest date on which a pharmacy may fill it. Three 30-day supplies stay within that total, and the later prescriptions are separate prescriptions, not refills.

Dating all three 3 March is correct, not a defect: 21 CFR 1306.05(a) requires every controlled-substance prescription to be dated as of, and signed on, the day when issued. The later fills are staged by the written instructions, not by later dates.

The request on 25 March fails on 21 CFR 1306.14(e): where a prescription prepared under 1306.12(b) contains the practitioner's instruction that it shall not be filled until a certain date, no pharmacist may fill it before that date. The trip does not change this, and Massachusetts guidance reports DEA's interpretation that no verbal modifications can be made to the earliest date on which the prescription may be filled, so a telephoned earlier date does not help.

The technician's count is the Massachusetts error. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) makes a Schedule II prescription invalid 30 days after the date of issuance, and Massachusetts guidance treats the do-not-fill-before date as the date of issuance for a prescription that carries one, with the date written remaining 3 March. The third prescription's 30 days therefore run from 2 May, and 12 May falls well inside them.

Methylphenidate is a non-opioid controlled substance, so M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d) would allow up to a 90-day supply upon a single filling; that ceiling does not let the pharmacy fill a prescription before its indicated date, and each prescription here orders a 30-day supply. The pharmacist filling each one endorses his or her own signature on its face under s. 23(c).
worked_examples.resolution: The second prescription cannot be filled before 2 April, and on the interpretation Massachusetts guidance reports, a telephoned change cannot move that date; the third may be filled on 12 May because for Massachusetts purposes its 30 days run from its do-not-fill-before date. The errors the scenario invites are counting the Massachusetts validity period from the date written on a staged prescription, and treating the earliest-fill date as something a patient's needs or a verbal change can move.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts pharmacist has three prescriptions, each written for a 90-day supply: methylphenidate for an adult with attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder, with no diagnosis recorded anywhere in the pharmacy's files; testosterone cypionate for a man with testosterone deficiency; and a buprenorphine buccal film prescribed for chronic pain. A colleague says the methylphenidate cannot go out as a 90-day fill until the diagnosis is verified, that the testosterone can because every Schedule III prescription may be filled for 90 days, and that the buprenorphine can because buprenorphine is the drug the statute names.
steps: Section 23(d) of M.G.L. c. 94C sorts Schedule II and III prescriptions into three 90-day categories, one defined by purpose, one by kind of drug and one by delivery system, and holds every other Schedule II or III prescription to a maximum of a 30-day supply upon a single filling.

Methylphenidate is a non-opioid controlled substance, and the statute names it as an example, so it may be filled for a maximum of a 90-day supply upon a single filling. Policy 2024-05 states that there is no longer a need to verify diagnoses for narcolepsy, attention deficit disorder or attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder, so the missing diagnosis is no bar.

Testosterone cypionate also falls in the category for non-opioid controlled substances, and the statute names testosterone. The colleague's reason is wrong even though the result is right: the schedule does not decide the category, and a Schedule III opioid outside the other categories is held to a 30-day supply upon a single filling.

The buprenorphine film is prescribed for pain, not for the treatment of opioid use disorder, and buprenorphine is an opioid, so on the statute's terms neither the opioid use disorder category nor the non-opioid category describes it. Because Policy 2024-05 gives buprenorphine products as its example of drugs for opioid use disorder, the course that is safe on either reading is to fill no more than a 30-day supply upon a single filling.

Whatever is done about the quantity written on the buprenorphine prescription, Policy 2024-05 states that changes to prescriptions for federally controlled drugs must be discussed with the prescriber, so any change to it goes through the prescriber.
worked_examples.resolution: The methylphenidate and the testosterone cypionate may each be filled for up to a 90-day supply, with no diagnosis check for the stimulant; the buprenorphine film for pain should not be filled for more than a 30-day supply upon a single filling. The error the scenario invites is sorting by schedule or by drug name instead of by the categories the statute actually uses.

worked_examples.scenario: A clonazepam prescription for 90 tablets, with no refills, is issued on 10 January. At the patient's request the pharmacy dispenses 30 tablets on 20 January and 30 more on 1 May. The patient returns on 15 July for the last 30 tablets, pointing out that six months have not yet passed since the first dispensing. After the patient leaves, a technician suggests removing the prescription from the files because it can no longer be used.
steps: Clonazepam is in Schedule IV, and 21 CFR 1306.23 makes the partial filling of a Schedule III, IV or V prescription permissible on three conditions, so staged dispensing was available from the start.

Each partial filling had to be recorded in the same manner as a refilling, and the total dispensed in all partial fillings may not exceed the 90 tablets prescribed; 30, 30 and a proposed 30 stay within that total.

The time condition is measured from issue: no dispensing may occur after 6 months after the date on which the prescription was issued. Six months after 10 January is 10 July, and 15 July falls after it, so the remaining tablets cannot be dispensed on this prescription however many are left.
The Massachusetts single-filling ceilings in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d) play no part, because that subsection speaks to Schedule II and III prescriptions and sets no maximum for Schedule IV.

The technician's suggestion fails under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(e): all prescriptions for controlled substances shall be kept for two years by the pharmacy and are subject to inspection under the chapter. The end of the period in which a prescription may be dispensed is not the end of the period for which it must be kept, and the federal retention floor taught with inventories and records applies alongside it.
worked_examples.resolution: The last 30 tablets cannot be dispensed on this prescription, and the prescription stays on file for two years. The errors the scenario invites are counting the six months from the first dispensing instead of from issue, and treating a prescription that can no longer be used as a record that can be discarded.

worked_examples.scenario: A practitioner in a Massachusetts outpatient office who is not registered to conduct a narcotic treatment program sees a patient with opioid use disorder on a Monday and counts a three-day supply of methadone out of the office's stock into a vial for the patient to take home, to initiate treatment while arranging referral to a narcotic treatment program. On Thursday the program still cannot admit the patient. The practitioner proposes either to hand over a second three-day supply or to give the patient a methadone prescription for maintenance to take to a community pharmacy. A colleague suggests a buprenorphine prescription instead and asks how large a supply a Massachusetts pharmacy could dispense on it in one filling.
steps: Start with the federal paragraph. 21 CFR 1306.07(b) lets a practitioner not specifically registered to conduct a narcotic treatment program dispense, but not prescribe, narcotic drugs to one person at one time to initiate maintenance or detoxification treatment, not more than a three-day supply at one time while arrangements are being made for referral, and only in accordance with applicable Federal, State, and local laws. Monday's supply fits the federal purpose and quantity, but the paragraph itself sends the question on to state law.

Apply the Massachusetts layer to Monday's supply. Under 105 CMR 700.010(A), other than for immediate administration, a practitioner shall not dispense controlled substances to an ultimate user in the course of professional practice except as sample medications, and a sample medication is a unit of prescription drug distributed by the manufacturer or distributor to practitioners in the original package from the manufacturer, not repackaged and given free of charge to patients; a supply counted out of the office's stock into a vial is repackaged and is not one. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(b) also confines a practitioner's dispensing to the quantity necessary for immediate and proper treatment until a prescription can be filled by a pharmacy. The take-home supply was therefore not available to this Massachusetts practitioner, even though it stayed within the federal three days, because the stricter rule governs.

A second three-day supply on Thursday is not available in any event. The paragraph provides that such emergency treatment may not be renewed or extended, and a further supply after the first renews or extends it, whatever the reason the referral is delayed.

The methadone prescription has no route either. Paragraph (b) excludes prescribing, and paragraph (a), which provides for maintenance or detoxification treatment with a Schedule II narcotic drug by a practitioner separately registered with DEA as a narcotic treatment program, permits administering or dispensing directly but not prescribing. A community pharmacy has no footing in 1306.07 for filling that prescription as an ordinary Schedule II prescription.

Buprenorphine is a Schedule III narcotic drug, and paragraph (d) lets a practitioner administer or dispense, including prescribe, any Schedule III, IV or V narcotic drug for use in maintenance or detoxification treatment to a narcotic dependent person, so the prescription route is open.

On the colleague's question, M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d) lets a Schedule II or III prescription for the treatment of opioid use disorder, including buprenorphine, be filled for a maximum of a 90-day supply upon a single filling, unless otherwise prohibited by statute. The ceiling is a maximum, not a quantity the prescription must carry.
worked_examples.resolution: In Massachusetts the take-home methadone supply on Monday was outside 105 CMR 700.010(A) from the start, whatever 21 CFR 1306.07(b) allows as a federal matter; a second supply is outside 1306.07(b) in any event; and the methadone prescription has no route. A buprenorphine prescription may be issued under paragraph (d), and a Massachusetts pharmacy may fill it for up to a 90-day supply upon a single filling. The error the scenario invites is reading the federal three-day paragraph as settling what a Massachusetts practitioner may hand a patient, treating the three-day ceiling as renewable, or treating a dispensing provision as though it opened a prescription route for methadone.

worked_examples.scenario: At the end of a day a Massachusetts pharmacy technician tidies the paperwork for two Schedule II prescriptions the pharmacy has filled, one written and one electronic. The technician files the written prescription with the day's Schedule III-V prescriptions, notes that the pharmacist's initials are already on both labels, and suggests that the electronic prescription needs no endorsement because it has no paper face. The manager separately proposes shredding written controlled-substance prescriptions that are 18 months old because none of them can be dispensed again.
steps: Section 23(c) of M.G.L. c. 94C places the endorsement on the pharmacist filling a written or electronic Schedule II prescription, who shall endorse his own signature on the face of it. Initials on a label are not a signature endorsed on the face of the prescription, so neither prescription has been endorsed.

The electronic prescription is not exempt, because the subsection names electronic prescriptions expressly. The text does not say how the face of an electronic prescription is endorsed, so the course that is safe on any reading is for the filling pharmacist's own signature to be endorsed on the electronic prescription record.
Section 23(b) requires written Schedule II prescriptions to be kept in a separate file, so the written prescription comes out of the Schedule III-V file and into a file of its own.

The shredding proposal fails under section 23(e): all prescriptions for controlled substances shall be kept for two years by the pharmacy and are subject to inspection under the chapter. Eighteen months is short of two years from any event the period could be counted from, and the subsection states no exception for prescriptions that can no longer be dispensed.
The federal retention floor for the same prescriptions is taught with inventories and records; where the two measures differ, the pharmacy keeps each prescription until the later period has run.
worked_examples.resolution: The filling pharmacist must endorse his or her own signature on both prescriptions, the written one goes into a separate Schedule II file, and nothing is shredded before two years have passed. The error the scenario invites is treating label initials as the statutory endorsement, and treating the end of a prescription's usefulness as the end of the duty to keep it.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Outside paragraphs (e), (f) and (g) of 21 CFR 1306.11, what must happen before a faxed paper Schedule II prescription can be dispensed?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The original manually signed prescription must be presented to the pharmacist for review prior to the actual dispensing; the fax on its own is only an advance copy.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which of the three fax-as-original paragraphs does not require a narcotic substance?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Paragraph (f), for a resident of a Long Term Care Facility, which reaches any Schedule II substance. Paragraphs (e) and (g) both require a Schedule II narcotic substance.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does 21 CFR 1306.11(g) require about the patient and about the prescription itself?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The patient must be enrolled in a hospice care program certified and/or paid for by Medicare under Title XVIII or a hospice program licensed by the state, and the practitioner or the practitioner's agent notes on the prescription that the patient is a hospice patient.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: the compounded-infusion fax exception applies only to patients in a hospital or facility.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. 21 CFR 1306.11(e) names no setting; it turns on a Schedule II narcotic substance to be compounded for direct administration to a patient by parenteral, intravenous, intramuscular, subcutaneous or intraspinal infusion.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who may send a fax that serves as the original under 21 CFR 1306.11(e), (f) or (g), and how is that fax kept?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The practitioner or the practitioner's agent; the facsimile is maintained in accordance with 21 CFR 1304.04(h).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 21 CFR 1306.12(b), who may issue multiple Schedule II prescriptions, and what is the ceiling on the set?
retrieval_prompts.answer: An individual practitioner; together the prescriptions may authorize the patient to receive a total of up to a 90-day supply.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which prescription in a multiple-prescription set may carry no earliest-fill instruction?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The first, if the prescribing practitioner intends it to be filled immediately. Each of the others carries written instructions indicating the earliest date on which a pharmacy may fill it.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: List the five conditions in 21 CFR 1306.12(b)(1).
retrieval_prompts.answer: Each prescription is issued for a legitimate medical purpose by an individual practitioner acting in the usual course of professional practice; written earliest-fill instructions appear on each prescription other than a first intended for immediate filling; the practitioner concludes there is no undue risk of diversion or abuse; the issuance is permissible under applicable state laws; and the practitioner complies fully with all other applicable requirements under the Act and the regulations, as well as any additional requirements under state law.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Does 21 CFR 1306.12(b) require or encourage practitioners to issue multiple Schedule II prescriptions?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. Paragraph (b)(2) says nothing in paragraph (b) mandates or encourages issuing multiple prescriptions or seeing patients only once every 90 days; the practitioner decides on sound medical judgment in accordance with established medical standards.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How is each prescription in a multiple Schedule II set dated?
retrieval_prompts.answer: As of, and signed on, the day when issued, under 21 CFR 1306.05(a). Every prescription issued at one visit bears that day's date; the later fills are staged by the practitioner's written earliest-fill instructions, not by later dates.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A patient asks a pharmacist to fill a later prescription in a multiple Schedule II set three days before the date its instruction indicates. What does 21 CFR 1306.14(e) provide?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No pharmacist may fill a prescription prepared under 21 CFR 1306.12(b) before the date the prescribing practitioner's instructions indicate.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: In Massachusetts, from what date does the 30-day validity of a later prescription in a multiple Schedule II set run?
retrieval_prompts.answer: From its do-not-fill-before date. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) makes a Schedule II prescription invalid 30 days after the date of issuance, and Massachusetts guidance treats the do-not-fill-before date as the date of issuance for a prescription that carries one; the date written remains the date it was written and signed. A Schedule II prescription from an out-of-state practitioner filled under s. 18(d) or (d1/2) runs instead on the five-day filling window taught with out-of-state prescriptions, and Board of Registration in Pharmacy guidance measures those five days from the do-not-fill-before date as well.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: a prescriber may telephone the pharmacy to move a later prescription's earliest-fill date forward.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False on the interpretation Massachusetts guidance reports from DEA: no verbal modifications can be made to the earliest date on which the Schedule II prescription may be filled.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: When does a written or electronic Schedule II prescription with no do-not-fill-before date become invalid in Massachusetts?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 30 days after the date of issuance, under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a). That is the working period for a Massachusetts prescriber's prescription; a Schedule II prescription from an out-of-state practitioner filled under s. 18(d) or (d1/2) may be filled only if it was issued within the preceding five days, as taught with out-of-state prescriptions.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: State the three conditions on which a Schedule III, IV or V prescription may be partially filled.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Each partial filling is recorded in the same manner as a refilling; the total quantity dispensed in all partial fillings does not exceed the total quantity prescribed; and no dispensing occurs after 6 months after the date on which the prescription was issued.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A Schedule IV prescription issued on 3 March is first partially filled on 1 May. From which date is the six-month limit counted?
retrieval_prompts.answer: From 3 March, the date of issue; the first partial filling on 1 May does not move it, so no dispensing may occur after six months after 3 March.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which Schedule II or III prescriptions may a Massachusetts pharmacy fill for up to a 90-day supply upon a single filling?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Unless otherwise prohibited by statute, prescriptions for the treatment of opioid use disorder, including buprenorphine; for non-opioid controlled substances, including methylphenidate and testosterone; and for implantable infusion pumps.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What is the Massachusetts maximum upon a single filling for any other Schedule II or III prescription, such as an opioid prescribed for pain?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A 30-day supply, under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: before filling a 90-day methylphenidate prescription, a Massachusetts pharmacist must verify a diagnosis of ADHD or narcolepsy.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. Policy 2024-05 states there is no longer a need to verify diagnoses for narcolepsy, attention deficit disorder or attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder, and methylphenidate is a non-opioid controlled substance within the 90-day category of M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Does M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d) set a single-filling maximum for a Schedule IV prescription?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. The subsection addresses Schedule II and III prescriptions only.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who endorses a Massachusetts Schedule II prescription, with what, and where?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The pharmacist filling the written or electronic prescription endorses his or her own signature on its face, under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(c).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which Schedule II prescriptions must be kept in a separate file under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(b)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Written Schedule II prescriptions.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How long, and by whom, are prescriptions for controlled substances kept under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(e)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: For two years, by the pharmacy, subject to inspection under chapter 94C.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 21 CFR 1306.07(b), what may a practitioner who is not registered to conduct a narcotic treatment program do, and within what limits?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Dispense, but not prescribe, narcotic drugs to one person or for one person's use at one time to initiate maintenance or detoxification treatment, in accordance with applicable Federal, State, and local laws; not more than a three-day supply at one time while arrangements are being made for referral; and the emergency treatment may not be renewed or extended. In Massachusetts, M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(b) and 105 CMR 700.010(A) also limit what a practitioner may dispense to an ultimate user.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 105 CMR 700.010(A), what may a Massachusetts practitioner dispense to an ultimate user, and what does the bar not reach?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Other than for immediate administration, a practitioner shall not dispense controlled substances to an ultimate user in the course of professional practice except as sample medications; for Schedule II through V the exception is a sample medication in a single dose or in such quantity as in the practitioner's opinion is essential for the immediate treatment of the patient. A sample medication is a unit of prescription drug distributed by the manufacturer or distributor in the original package, not repackaged and given free of charge. The bar is stated as applying other than for immediate administration.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(b), how much may a practitioner dispense to an ultimate user, and how are the rest of the patient's controlled substances to be supplied?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A single dose or a quantity the practitioner considers essential for treatment, not exceeding the quantity necessary for the immediate and proper treatment of the patient until it is possible for the patient to have a prescription filled by a pharmacy; all controlled substances required by the patient as part of the patient's treatment shall be dispensed by prescription to the ultimate user in accordance with chapter 94C.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which paragraph of 21 CFR 1306.07 lets a practitioner prescribe for maintenance or detoxification treatment, and for which drugs?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Paragraph (d): a practitioner may administer or dispense, including prescribe, any Schedule III, IV or V narcotic drug for use in maintenance or detoxification treatment to a narcotic dependent person.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 21 CFR 1306.07(a), what may a narcotic treatment program practitioner do with a Schedule II narcotic drug, and on what two conditions?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Administer or dispense directly, but not prescribe, to a narcotic dependent person for maintenance or detoxification treatment, if separately registered with DEA as a narcotic treatment program and in compliance with DEA regulations regarding treatment qualifications, security, records, and unsupervised use of the drugs.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A pharmacy delivers a Schedule III narcotic drug for maintenance treatment by injection to a practitioner under 21 CFR 1306.07(f). By when must it be administered, and to whom?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Only to the patient named on the prescription, not later than 45 days after the date the practitioner receives it.

quick_review.text: Outside paragraphs (e), (f) and (g) of 21 CFR 1306.11, a faxed paper Schedule II prescription is an advance copy: the original manually signed prescription must be presented to the pharmacist for review prior to the actual dispensing.

A fax serves as the original written prescription for a Schedule II narcotic substance to be compounded for direct parenteral, intravenous, intramuscular, subcutaneous or intraspinal infusion, whatever the setting.
A fax serves as the original for a Schedule II substance, narcotic or not, for a resident of a Long Term Care Facility.

A fax serves as the original for a Schedule II narcotic substance for a patient enrolled in a hospice care program certified and/or paid for by Medicare under Title XVIII or a state-licensed hospice program, with the practitioner or agent noting on the prescription that the patient is a hospice patient.
Each fax that serves as the original is prepared in accordance with 21 CFR 1306.05, sent by the practitioner or the practitioner's agent, and maintained in accordance with 21 CFR 1304.04(h).

An individual practitioner may issue multiple Schedule II prescriptions authorizing a total of up to a 90-day supply, each for a legitimate medical purpose in the usual course of professional practice, with written earliest-fill instructions on each prescription other than a first intended for immediate filling.

The multiple-prescription permission also requires the practitioner to conclude there is no undue risk of diversion or abuse, and depends on state law permitting it and on full compliance with all other applicable requirements under the Act and the regulations and any additional requirements under state law.
Nothing in 21 CFR 1306.12(b) mandates or encourages multiple prescriptions or 90-day visit intervals, and refilling a Schedule II prescription remains prohibited.
Every prescription in a multiple Schedule II set is dated as of, and signed on, the day when issued, and no pharmacist may fill a later one before the date the practitioner's instruction indicates.

In Massachusetts a written or electronic Schedule II prescription becomes invalid 30 days after the date of issuance, and for a prescription carrying a do-not-fill-before date Massachusetts guidance treats that date as the date of issuance. A Schedule II prescription from an out-of-state practitioner filled under s. 18(d) or (d1/2) may be filled only if issued within the preceding five days, and Board of Registration in Pharmacy guidance measures those five days from the do-not-fill-before date where there is one.

A Schedule III, IV or V prescription may be partially filled if each partial filling is recorded in the same manner as a refilling, the total stays within the quantity prescribed, and nothing is dispensed after six months after the issue date.

In Massachusetts a Schedule II or III prescription for the treatment of opioid use disorder, for a non-opioid controlled substance, or for an implantable infusion pump may be filled for a maximum of a 90-day supply upon a single filling, unless otherwise prohibited by statute.

Every other Schedule II or III prescription, such as an opioid prescribed for pain, may be filled for a maximum of a 30-day supply upon a single filling; M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d) sets no maximum for Schedule IV or V.

Policy 2024-05 applies to all pharmacies that dispense into, within, or from Massachusetts, states there is no longer a need to verify narcolepsy or attention-deficit diagnoses, and says changes to prescriptions for federally controlled drugs must be discussed with the prescriber.

The pharmacist filling a written or electronic Schedule II prescription endorses his or her own signature on its face, written Schedule II prescriptions are kept in a separate file, and a written or electronic Schedule II prescription shall not be refilled.
All prescriptions for controlled substances are kept for two years by the pharmacy and are subject to inspection under chapter 94C.

Under 21 CFR 1306.07(a) a practitioner separately registered with DEA as a narcotic treatment program may administer or dispense directly, but not prescribe, a Schedule II narcotic drug for maintenance or detoxification treatment.

Under 21 CFR 1306.07(b) a practitioner not registered to conduct a narcotic treatment program may dispense, but not prescribe, not more than a three-day supply at one time to initiate treatment while referral is arranged, and may not renew or extend that emergency treatment.

In Massachusetts, 105 CMR 700.010(A) bars a practitioner, other than for immediate administration, from dispensing controlled substances to an ultimate user except as sample medications, and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(b) limits a practitioner's dispensing to the quantity necessary for immediate and proper treatment until a prescription can be filled by a pharmacy; 21 CFR 1306.07(b) requires compliance with both.
Under 21 CFR 1306.07(d) a practitioner may administer or dispense, including prescribe, a Schedule III, IV or V narcotic drug for maintenance or detoxification treatment.

Under 21 CFR 1306.07(f) a pharmacy may deliver a Schedule III, IV or V narcotic drug for maintenance or detoxification treatment by injection or implantation to the practitioner's registered location, for administration only to the named patient not later than 45 days after the practitioner receives it.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule II prescription arrives by fax.
decision_logic.action: Check that it came from the practitioner or the practitioner's agent and whether 21 CFR 1306.11(e), (f) or (g) applies. If none does, treat the fax as an advance copy and dispense only after the pharmacist has reviewed the original manually signed prescription.

decision_logic.condition: The faxed Schedule II prescription is for a resident of a Long Term Care Facility.
decision_logic.action: Treat the fax as the original written prescription under paragraph (f), whether or not the drug is a narcotic, and maintain it in accordance with 21 CFR 1304.04(h).

decision_logic.condition: The faxed Schedule II prescription is for a hospice patient.
decision_logic.action: Confirm a Schedule II narcotic substance, enrolment in a hospice care program certified and/or paid for by Medicare under Title XVIII or a state-licensed hospice program, and the practitioner's or agent's note that the patient is a hospice patient. If the note is missing, obtain a prescription carrying it from the practitioner's side, or the original, before dispensing.

decision_logic.condition: The faxed Schedule II prescription is for a drug to be compounded for infusion.
decision_logic.action: Confirm a Schedule II narcotic substance to be compounded for direct administration by parenteral, intravenous, intramuscular, subcutaneous or intraspinal infusion; if so, the fax serves as the original under paragraph (e) wherever the patient is.

decision_logic.condition: A faxed Schedule II prescription is to be filled in Massachusetts.
decision_logic.action: Decide separately, under the Massachusetts electronic-prescribing and written-format rules taught with Massachusetts oral prescriptions, whether a non-electronic prescription may be accepted at all, apply the stricter rule, and keep a fax that serves as the original in the separate Schedule II file.

decision_logic.condition: A patient presents several Schedule II prescriptions issued together.
decision_logic.action: Confirm that each is a separate prescription dated as of, and signed on, the day it was issued, that together they authorize no more than a 90-day supply, and that each one after a first intended for immediate filling carries a written earliest-fill instruction; fill none before its indicated date.

decision_logic.condition: Someone asks the pharmacist to split one Schedule II prescription into several prescriptions, or to add refills to it.
decision_logic.action: Decline. Refilling a Schedule II prescription is prohibited, and multiple prescriptions are issued by the individual practitioner, whose judgments 21 CFR 1306.12(b) requires. A patient's request that one Schedule II prescription be dispensed in a lesser quantity is a different request: it is a partial filling, which 21 CFR 1306.13(b) permits on its conditions and for which M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) provides that a pharmacist filling a Schedule II prescription shall, if requested by the patient, dispense a lesser quantity; Schedule II partial fills are taught in their own section.

decision_logic.condition: A patient asks for a later prescription in a set to be filled before its indicated date, or says the prescriber will telephone an earlier date.
decision_logic.action: Do not fill it before the indicated date: under 21 CFR 1306.14(e) no pharmacist may, and Massachusetts guidance reports DEA's interpretation that no verbal modifications can be made to the earliest date on which the prescription may be filled.

decision_logic.condition: A prescription from a multiple Schedule II set is presented to a Massachusetts pharmacy on or after its indicated date.
decision_logic.action: Treat it as invalid 30 days after its date of issuance under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a), taking its do-not-fill-before date as the date of issuance, as Massachusetts guidance does for a Massachusetts prescriber's prescriptions, and hold the filling to the single-filling ceiling in s. 23(d). If the prescriber is an out-of-state practitioner whose prescription is filled under s. 18(d) or (d1/2), each of which authorizes the filling only of prescriptions issued within the preceding five days, fill it only within those five days, counting them from the prescription's do-not-fill-before date where it has one, as Board of Registration in Pharmacy guidance does for a nonresident prescriber's Schedule II prescriptions, and only if the other out-of-state conditions taught with out-of-state prescriptions are met.

decision_logic.condition: A patient asks for part of the quantity on a Schedule III, IV or V prescription.
decision_logic.action: Dispense the part if the conditions of 21 CFR 1306.23 can be kept: record each partial filling in the same manner as a refilling, keep the running total within the quantity prescribed, and dispense nothing after six months after the issue date.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule II or III prescription is to be filled in Massachusetts.
decision_logic.action: Classify it first. For the treatment of opioid use disorder, a non-opioid controlled substance or an implantable infusion pump, the ceiling is a 90-day supply upon a single filling unless otherwise prohibited by statute; any other Schedule II or III prescription is capped at a 30-day supply upon a single filling.

decision_logic.condition: A quantity question arises on a Schedule IV or V prescription.
decision_logic.action: Do not apply M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d), which sets no single-filling maximum for those schedules; look to the other rules that govern the prescription.

decision_logic.condition: The quantity on a Schedule II or III prescription exceeds the Massachusetts ceiling for its category.
decision_logic.action: Do not dispense more than the ceiling upon a single filling, and discuss any change to the prescription with the prescriber, as Policy 2024-05 states for federally controlled drugs.

decision_logic.condition: A pharmacist fills a written or electronic Schedule II prescription in Massachusetts.
decision_logic.action: Endorse the filling pharmacist's own signature on its face, and keep a written prescription in the separate Schedule II file.

decision_logic.condition: Someone proposes to discard a prescription for a controlled substance.
decision_logic.action: Keep it for two years under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(e). Where the starting point matters, count from the last dispensing on the prescription, and where the federal floor taught with inventories and records ends later, keep it until then.

decision_logic.condition: A prescription for a Schedule II narcotic drug is for maintenance or detoxification treatment.
decision_logic.action: Do not fill it as an ordinary Schedule II prescription: no paragraph of 21 CFR 1306.07 provides for prescribing a Schedule II narcotic drug for that purpose.

decision_logic.condition: A prescription for a Schedule III, IV or V narcotic drug is for maintenance or detoxification treatment.
decision_logic.action: Treat it as within 21 CFR 1306.07(d), which includes prescribing. In Massachusetts a Schedule III prescription for the treatment of opioid use disorder may, unless otherwise prohibited by statute, be filled for a maximum of a 90-day supply upon a single filling; M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d) sets no single-filling maximum for Schedule IV or V.

decision_logic.condition: A practitioner not registered to conduct a narcotic treatment program wants to supply more narcotic medication after an initial emergency supply.
decision_logic.action: Treat the further supply as outside 21 CFR 1306.07(b), which allows not more than a three-day supply at one time while referral is arranged and provides that the emergency treatment may not be renewed or extended.

decision_logic.condition: A Massachusetts practitioner not registered to conduct a narcotic treatment program proposes to hand a patient a take-home supply of methadone to initiate treatment.
decision_logic.action: Do not treat 21 CFR 1306.07(b) as settling it. That paragraph requires compliance with State law, 105 CMR 700.010(A) bars a practitioner, other than for immediate administration, from dispensing controlled substances to an ultimate user except as sample medications, and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(b) confines a practitioner's dispensing to what immediate and proper treatment requires until a prescription can be filled by a pharmacy; a supply counted out of office stock is repackaged and is not a sample medication as 105 CMR 700.001 defines it.

decision_logic.condition: A practitioner asks the pharmacy to deliver a Schedule III, IV or V narcotic drug for injection or implantation for maintenance or detoxification treatment.
decision_logic.action: Deliver under 21 CFR 1306.07(f) only if every condition is met: a prescription meeting 21 CFR 1306.04, delivery at the location on the practitioner's DEA certificate of registration, authority under State law, no stock for general dispensing, administration only to the named patient not later than 45 days after receipt, and the practitioners' records.

ma_vs_federal.text: A federal fax exception settles only whether the facsimile may serve as the original written prescription under 21 CFR 1306.11. On Massachusetts facts the Massachusetts electronic-prescribing and written-format rules, taught with Massachusetts oral prescriptions, decide whether a non-electronic Schedule II prescription may be accepted at all, and the stricter rule governs.

21 CFR 1306.12(b)(1)(iv) and (v) make the federal multiple-prescription permission depend on state law. Massachusetts guidance records the determination of the Drug Control Program and the Board of Registration in Pharmacy that issuing multiple Schedule II prescriptions in accordance with the federal regulation is permissible under chapter 94C, and it measures each prescription's 30-day validity under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) from its do-not-fill-before date.

Federal law stages a set by dating every prescription on the day it is issued and forbidding any pharmacist to fill a later one before its indicated date; Massachusetts then asks whether each prescription is still valid and whether each filling is within the s. 23(d) ceiling. Both apply, so a later prescription is filled on or after its indicated date, before it becomes invalid, and within the ceiling.

The federal 90 days in 21 CFR 1306.12(b) is a total across a set of prescriptions issued by a practitioner; the Massachusetts figures in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d) are ceilings on each single filling. Both apply, so a set within the federal total is still filled one ceiling-compliant filling at a time.

21 CFR 1306.23 governs the partial filling of Schedule III-V prescriptions as a federal matter; for a Schedule III prescription filled in Massachusetts, each partial filling is also held to the single-filling ceiling in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d).

The endorsement in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(c) and the separate file in s. 23(b) are Massachusetts duties on the Schedule II prescriptions a Massachusetts pharmacy fills, including a facsimile that federal law treats as the original; the federal recordkeeping rules for the same prescriptions apply alongside them.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(e) requires the pharmacy to keep controlled-substance prescriptions for two years; the federal retention floor, taught with inventories and records, is measured on its own terms, and where both reach the same prescription the pharmacy keeps it until the later period ends.

21 CFR 1306.07 decides who may treat a narcotic dependent person with which narcotic drugs and by what action, and paragraph (b) allows its three-day dispensing only in accordance with applicable State law. Massachusetts reaches the same act more strictly: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(b) confines a practitioner's dispensing to an ultimate user to the quantity necessary for the immediate and proper treatment of the patient until a prescription can be filled by a pharmacy, and 105 CMR 700.010(A) bars a practitioner, other than for immediate administration, from dispensing controlled substances to an ultimate user except as sample medications, so a Massachusetts office practitioner may not hand a patient a take-home supply of methadone that is not a sample medication, and the stricter rule governs. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d) separately decides how much a lawful Schedule II or III prescription for the treatment of opioid use disorder may supply in one filling, and it adds no route.

exceptions.text: Paragraphs (e), (f) and (g) of 21 CFR 1306.11 are the exceptions to the requirement that the original manually signed prescription be presented to the pharmacist before the actual dispensing of a faxed Schedule II prescription.

Separately, 21 CFR 1306.11(a) excepts from its written-prescription requirement the emergency oral dispensing provided for in paragraph (d), which is taught with emergency oral Schedule II dispensing and its follow-up.
The first prescription of a multiple-prescription set needs no earliest-fill instruction if the practitioner intends it to be filled immediately.

The 90-day categories in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d) apply unless otherwise prohibited by statute, so a stricter statutory limit, such as a limit on an initial opioid prescription where it applies, still controls.

The department may provide by regulation for a single-filling maximum of less than a 90-day supply for a Schedule II or III substance if the secretary of health and human services or the board of pharmacy determines that the restriction is needed to address increased abuse of the substance.

21 CFR 1306.07(b) is a limited exception for a practitioner not registered to conduct a narcotic treatment program: dispensing but not prescribing, not more than a three-day supply at one time, to initiate treatment while referral is arranged, with no renewal or extension, and only in accordance with applicable State law, which in Massachusetts includes M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(b) and 105 CMR 700.010(A).

105 CMR 700.010(A) states its bar on a practitioner's dispensing to an ultimate user as applying other than for immediate administration, and excepts only sample medications, for Schedule II through V in a single dose or in such quantity as in the practitioner's opinion is essential for the immediate treatment of the patient.

21 CFR 1306.07(c) states that the section is not intended to limit a physician or authorized hospital staff in administering or dispensing narcotic drugs in a hospital as an incidental adjunct to medical or surgical treatment of conditions other than addiction, or in administering or dispensing narcotic drugs to persons with intractable pain.

21 CFR 1306.07(f) operates notwithstanding the Act's definition of dispense, allowing a pharmacy to deliver a Schedule III, IV or V narcotic drug to a practitioner for administration by injection or implantation, on its six conditions.
M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(e) states no exception to the two-year retention of prescriptions for controlled substances.

timing_deadlines.event: Actual dispensing of a faxed Schedule II prescription outside 21 CFR 1306.11(e)-(g)
timing_deadlines.consequence: The original manually signed prescription must have been presented to the pharmacist for review; until then nothing is dispensed on the fax.

timing_deadlines.event: Dating and signing each prescription in a multiple Schedule II set
timing_deadlines.timeframe: As of, and on, the day when issued
timing_deadlines.consequence: Every prescription issued at one visit bears that day's date, and the later fills are staged by the practitioner's written earliest-fill instructions.

timing_deadlines.event: Filling a later prescription in a multiple-prescription set
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not before the earliest date indicated in the practitioner's written instruction
timing_deadlines.consequence: No pharmacist may fill it before that date under 21 CFR 1306.14(e), and Massachusetts guidance reports DEA's interpretation that the date cannot be modified verbally.

timing_deadlines.event: Total supply authorized by a set of multiple Schedule II prescriptions
timing_deadlines.consequence: A set authorizing more is outside 21 CFR 1306.12(b)(1).

timing_deadlines.event: Validity of a written or electronic Schedule II prescription in Massachusetts
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Invalid 30 days after the date of issuance
timing_deadlines.consequence: For a prescription carrying a do-not-fill-before date, Massachusetts guidance treats that date as the date of issuance, so the 30 days run from it; otherwise they run from the date the prescription was issued. A Schedule II prescription from an out-of-state practitioner filled under s. 18(d) or (d1/2) may be filled only if it was issued within the preceding five days, as taught with out-of-state prescriptions, and Board of Registration in Pharmacy guidance measures those five days in the same way, from the do-not-fill-before date where there is one and otherwise from the date of issuance.

timing_deadlines.event: Partial filling of a Schedule III, IV or V prescription
timing_deadlines.timeframe: No dispensing after 6 months after the date the prescription was issued
timing_deadlines.consequence: The remaining quantity cannot be dispensed on that prescription, however much remains.

timing_deadlines.event: Single filling of a Massachusetts Schedule II or III prescription for the treatment of opioid use disorder, a non-opioid controlled substance or an implantable infusion pump
timing_deadlines.consequence: No more may be dispensed upon that filling, and a lower figure set by statute or by department regulation controls where one applies.

timing_deadlines.event: Single filling of any other Massachusetts Schedule II or III prescription
timing_deadlines.consequence: No more may be dispensed upon that filling.

timing_deadlines.event: Retention of a prescription for a controlled substance
timing_deadlines.consequence: The pharmacy keeps the prescription, subject to inspection under chapter 94C; the starting event is not stated, and counting from the last dispensing is safe on any reading.

timing_deadlines.event: Dispensing by a practitioner not registered to conduct a narcotic treatment program to initiate treatment
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not more than a three-day supply at one time, while arrangements are being made for referral
timing_deadlines.consequence: The emergency treatment may not be renewed or extended; in Massachusetts, M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(b) and 105 CMR 700.010(A) also limit a practitioner's dispensing to an ultimate user.

timing_deadlines.event: Administration of a Schedule III, IV or V narcotic drug delivered by a pharmacy under 21 CFR 1306.07(f)
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not later than 45 days after the practitioner receives it
timing_deadlines.consequence: It is administered only to the patient named on the prescription, within that period.

forms_records.text: A facsimile that serves as the original written prescription under 21 CFR 1306.11(e), (f) or (g) is maintained in accordance with 21 CFR 1304.04(h); outside those paragraphs it is the original manually signed prescription that is maintained in that way.

Each fax-as-original prescription is prepared in accordance with 21 CFR 1306.05, and under paragraph (g) the practitioner or the practitioner's agent notes on it that the patient is a hospice patient.

Every controlled-substance prescription is dated as of, and signed on, the day when issued and bears the patient's full name and address, the drug name, strength, dosage form, quantity prescribed, directions for use, and the practitioner's name, address and registration number.

In a set of multiple Schedule II prescriptions, each prescription other than a first intended for immediate filling carries the practitioner's written instructions indicating the earliest date on which a pharmacy may fill it, and that written date is the one no pharmacist may fill before.
Each partial filling of a Schedule III, IV or V prescription is recorded in the same manner as a refilling; the refill record itself is taught with Schedule III-V refills and transfers.

The pharmacist filling a written or electronic Schedule II prescription endorses his or her own signature on the face of the prescription; initials on a label are not a signature endorsed on its face.

Written Schedule II prescriptions are kept in a separate file under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(b), and a facsimile that federal law treats as the original written prescription can be kept in that file on any reading.
Every prescription for a controlled substance is kept by the pharmacy for two years and is subject to inspection under chapter 94C.

Policy 2024-05 states that there is no longer a need to verify diagnoses for narcolepsy, attention deficit disorder or attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder, so no diagnosis record is a condition of filling a stimulant within the 90-day category.

A practitioner acting under 21 CFR 1306.07(a) must be separately registered with DEA as a narcotic treatment program and in compliance with DEA regulations regarding records, as well as treatment qualifications, security and unsupervised use of the drugs.

Under 21 CFR 1306.07(f)(6) the prescribing and administering practitioners, as applicable, maintain complete and accurate records of all controlled substances delivered, received, administered or otherwise disposed of under the paragraph, including the persons to whom they were delivered.

role_duties.role: Prescribing practitioner or the practitioner's agent sending a Schedule II fax
role_duties.duty: Transmit a prescription prepared in accordance with 21 CFR 1306.05, and for a hospice patient under paragraph (g) note on the prescription that the patient is a hospice patient.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist receiving a faxed Schedule II prescription
role_duties.duty: Review the original manually signed prescription before the actual dispensing unless the fax qualifies under 21 CFR 1306.11(e), (f) or (g), and maintain whichever document is the original in accordance with 21 CFR 1304.04(h).

role_duties.role: Individual practitioner issuing multiple Schedule II prescriptions
role_duties.duty: Issue each prescription for a legitimate medical purpose in the usual course of professional practice, keep the set within a total of a 90-day supply, write earliest-fill instructions on each prescription other than a first intended for immediate filling, conclude that the set creates no undue risk of diversion or abuse, and comply with state law and all other applicable requirements.
Date the prescription as of, and sign it on, the day when issued, and include the patient, drug, quantity, directions and practitioner information 21 CFR 1306.05(a) requires.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist presented with a prescription from a multiple-prescription set
role_duties.duty: Treat it as a separate prescription rather than a refill, and do not fill it before the date the practitioner's written instruction indicates.

role_duties.role: Massachusetts pharmacist filling a prescription from a multiple Schedule II set
role_duties.duty: Treat the prescription as invalid 30 days after its date of issuance under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a), taking its do-not-fill-before date as that date, as Massachusetts guidance does for a Massachusetts prescriber's prescriptions; for a prescription from an out-of-state practitioner filled under s. 18(d) or (d1/2), each of which authorizes the filling only of prescriptions issued within the preceding five days, fill it only within those five days, counting them from its do-not-fill-before date where it has one, as Board of Registration in Pharmacy guidance does for a nonresident prescriber's Schedule II prescriptions.

role_duties.role: Pharmacy partially filling a Schedule III, IV or V prescription
role_duties.duty: Record each partial filling in the same manner as a refilling, keep the total within the quantity prescribed, and dispense nothing after six months after the date the prescription was issued.

role_duties.role: Massachusetts pharmacist filling a Schedule II or III prescription
role_duties.duty: Classify the prescription under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d), dispense no more than the applicable 90-day or 30-day supply upon a single filling, and discuss any change to a prescription for a federally controlled drug with the prescriber, as Policy 2024-05 states.

May provide by regulation that a Schedule II or III substance may be filled for a maximum of less than a 90-day supply upon a single filling, where the secretary of health and human services or the board of pharmacy has determined that the restriction is needed to address increased abuse.

role_duties.role: Secretary of health and human services or board of pharmacy
role_duties.duty: Determine whether a restriction below a 90-day supply is needed to address increased abuse of a Schedule II or III substance, the determination on which a department regulation lowering the ceiling depends.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist filling a Massachusetts Schedule II prescription
role_duties.duty: Endorse his or her own signature on the face of the written or electronic prescription.

role_duties.role: Pharmacy holding written Schedule II prescriptions
role_duties.duty: Keep written Schedule II prescriptions in a separate file; M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(b) states the requirement without naming an actor, and it is met where the prescriptions are held.

role_duties.role: Pharmacy keeping prescriptions for controlled substances
role_duties.duty: Keep every prescription for a controlled substance for two years, subject to inspection under chapter 94C, counting from the last dispensing on it where the starting point matters.

role_duties.role: Practitioner registered with DEA as a narcotic treatment program
role_duties.duty: Administer or dispense Schedule II narcotic drugs for maintenance or detoxification treatment directly and not by prescription, in compliance with DEA regulations regarding treatment qualifications, security, records, and unsupervised use of the drugs.

role_duties.role: Practitioner not registered to conduct a narcotic treatment program
role_duties.duty: Dispense, not prescribe, not more than a three-day supply of narcotic drugs at one time to initiate treatment while referral is arranged, in accordance with applicable Federal, State, and local laws, and do not renew or extend that emergency treatment. In Massachusetts, also apply 105 CMR 700.010(A) and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 9(b): other than for immediate administration, do not dispense controlled substances to an ultimate user except as sample medications, and keep any dispensing within what immediate treatment requires until a prescription can be filled by a pharmacy.

role_duties.role: Practitioner treating with a Schedule III, IV or V narcotic drug
role_duties.duty: Administer, dispense or prescribe the drug for maintenance or detoxification treatment of a narcotic dependent person under 21 CFR 1306.07(d).

Deliver a Schedule III, IV or V narcotic drug for injection or implantation only pursuant to a prescription that meets 21 CFR 1306.04, only to the prescribing or administering practitioner at the location listed on the practitioner's DEA certificate of registration, and only where State law authorizes the activity and the prescription is not issued to supply a stock for general dispensing.

role_duties.role: Prescribing or administering practitioner receiving a delivery under 21 CFR 1306.07(f)
role_duties.duty: Administer the drug only to the patient named on the prescription not later than 45 days after receiving it, and keep complete and accurate records of all controlled substances delivered, received, administered or otherwise disposed of under the paragraph.

common_traps.text: Treating every faxed Schedule II prescription as an original. Outside 21 CFR 1306.11(e), (f) and (g) the original manually signed prescription must be reviewed before the actual dispensing.

Believing a Schedule II prescription may not be sent by fax at all. Paragraph (a) permits transmission by facsimile; what it withholds, outside the three exceptions, is the fax's standing as the original.

Carrying the narcotic condition of the infusion and hospice paragraphs into the Long Term Care Facility paragraph, which reaches a Schedule II substance for a resident whether or not it is a narcotic.

Relying on hospice status alone. Paragraph (g) also requires a Schedule II narcotic substance, a hospice program certified and/or paid for by Medicare or licensed by the state, and the practitioner's or agent's note that the patient is a hospice patient.

Reading a federal fax exception as settling whether Massachusetts accepts a non-electronic prescription; the Massachusetts electronic-prescribing and written-format rules, taught with Massachusetts oral prescriptions, decide that separately.
Calling the later prescriptions in a multiple-prescription set refills, or reading the 90 days as a supply for each prescription rather than the total for the set.
Postdating the later prescriptions in a set; each prescription is dated as of, and signed on, the day it is issued, and the fills are staged by written earliest-fill instructions.

Filling a later prescription early because the patient asks, because a Massachusetts ceiling would allow the combined quantity, or because the prescriber telephones a new date; no pharmacist may fill it before the indicated date, and Massachusetts guidance reports DEA's interpretation that the date cannot be modified verbally.

Counting the Massachusetts 30-day validity of a later prescription in a set from the date written; Massachusetts guidance treats its do-not-fill-before date as the date of issuance under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23. The 30-day period is not the window for a Schedule II prescription from an out-of-state practitioner filled under s. 18(d) or (d1/2), which may be filled only if issued within the preceding five days, and counting those five days from the date written is the same mistake: Board of Registration in Pharmacy guidance measures them from the do-not-fill-before date where there is one.
Counting the Schedule III-V six-month limit from the first partial filling instead of from the date the prescription was issued.
Believing a partial filling adds quantity or time; the total across all partial fillings may not exceed the quantity prescribed, and the six months still run from issue.
Reading the Massachusetts 30-day supply ceiling as a 30-day validity period; M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d) measures the supply dispensed upon a single filling, while s. 23(a) measures validity.

Assuming every Schedule III prescription may be filled for 90 days; the 90-day ceiling reaches only the opioid use disorder, non-opioid and implantable infusion pump categories, and a Schedule III opioid for pain is held to a 30-day supply.
Applying M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d) to Schedule IV or V prescriptions, which it does not address.
Holding a stimulant to 30 days until a diagnosis is verified; Policy 2024-05 states there is no longer a need to verify narcolepsy or attention-deficit diagnoses.
Taking the prescriber's signature, or initials on a label, as the endorsement; M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(c) requires the filling pharmacist's own signature on the face of the prescription.
Treating an electronic Schedule II prescription as exempt from endorsement because it has no paper face; the subsection names electronic prescriptions.
Discarding a controlled-substance prescription once it can no longer be filled or refilled; M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(e) requires the pharmacy to keep it for two years.
Reading 21 CFR 1306.07(b) as a prescription route, or its three-day supply as renewable; it permits dispensing but not prescribing, and the emergency treatment may not be renewed or extended.

Reading 21 CFR 1306.07(b) as settling what a Massachusetts practitioner may hand a patient to take home. The paragraph requires compliance with State law, and 105 CMR 700.010(A) bars a practitioner's dispensing to an ultimate user, other than for immediate administration, except as sample medications.

Relying on older materials that describe a limit of one day's medication at a time, or an exception request to DEA to reach three days; the current paragraph itself allows not more than a three-day supply to be dispensed at one time.

Sending buprenorphine maintenance or detoxification treatment through the narcotic treatment program route, when 21 CFR 1306.07(d) lets a practitioner prescribe a Schedule III, IV or V narcotic drug for that purpose.

Treating a methadone prescription for maintenance treatment like a methadone prescription for pain; the purpose decides whether the maintenance and detoxification limits of 21 CFR 1306.07 apply at all.
Measuring the 45 days in 21 CFR 1306.07(f) from the date of the prescription instead of from the practitioner's receipt of the drug.
Treating the Massachusetts 90-day opioid use disorder category as authority to fill a methadone maintenance prescription; the state ceiling adds no route that 21 CFR 1306.07 does not provide.

drug_examples.teaching_point: A Schedule II stimulant that is not a narcotic: a faxed prescription can serve as the original for a Long Term Care Facility resident under 21 CFR 1306.11(f), but not under the hospice or compounded-infusion paragraphs, which require a narcotic substance; in Massachusetts it is a non-opioid controlled substance named in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d) and may be filled for up to a 90-day supply upon a single filling.

A Schedule II opioid: a faxed prescription for a patient enrolled in a qualifying hospice program, with the hospice note, can serve as the original; prescribed for pain in Massachusetts it may be filled for no more than a 30-day supply upon a single filling, including each prescription in a multiple-prescription set.
A Schedule II narcotic: a faxed prescription for fentanyl to be compounded for direct intravenous infusion can serve as the original under 21 CFR 1306.11(e), whatever the setting.

A Schedule II narcotic: a faxed prescription for hydromorphone to be compounded for subcutaneous or intraspinal infusion fits 21 CFR 1306.11(e), while a faxed tablet prescription for an ambulatory patient fits none of the three paragraphs.

A Schedule III non-opioid named in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d): up to a 90-day supply upon a single filling in Massachusetts, and its prescription may be partially filled under 21 CFR 1306.23, with no dispensing after six months after issue.

Acetaminophen-codeine tablets, a Schedule III opioid combination: prescribed for pain they fall in none of the 90-day categories, so a Massachusetts filling may be for no more than a 30-day supply, and any partial fillings under 21 CFR 1306.23 stay within the quantity prescribed and end six months after issue.

A Schedule IV benzodiazepine: no partial filling under 21 CFR 1306.23 may be dispensed after six months after issue, M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d) sets no single-filling maximum for it, and its prescription is kept for two years under s. 23(e).

A Schedule II opioid whatever it is prescribed for: for maintenance or detoxification treatment it is administered or dispensed directly by a narcotic treatment program under 21 CFR 1306.07(a), and 1306.07 gives no route to prescribe it for that purpose; paragraph (b) lets a practitioner not registered as a narcotic treatment program dispense an initiating supply of not more than three days only in accordance with State law, and in Massachusetts 105 CMR 700.010(A) bars a practitioner, other than for immediate administration, from dispensing controlled substances to an ultimate user except as sample medications, so a take-home supply counted out of an office practitioner's stock, which is repackaged and not a sample medication, is not available; for pain it is dispensed under the ordinary Schedule II rules, with a 30-day ceiling upon a single filling in Massachusetts.

A Schedule III narcotic drug: a practitioner may prescribe it for maintenance or detoxification treatment under 21 CFR 1306.07(d), and a Massachusetts prescription for the treatment of opioid use disorder may be filled for up to a 90-day supply upon a single filling.

A Schedule III narcotic combination product: it may be prescribed for maintenance or detoxification treatment under 21 CFR 1306.07(d), and filled in Massachusetts for up to a 90-day supply upon a single filling when prescribed for opioid use disorder.

A Schedule III extended-release buprenorphine injection for opioid use disorder: a pharmacy may deliver it to the prescribing or administering practitioner under 21 CFR 1306.07(f), for administration only to the named patient not later than 45 days after the practitioner receives it.
